original_question: Consider a semi-algebraic set in R^k defined by l quadratic inequalities. Can the number of connected components of such a set be computed by an algorithm with complexity k^O(l), or even k^O(l^2), rather than the currently best known k^(2^O(l)) type bound coming from the available all-Betti-number methods? Equivalently, is there a substantially more efficient algorithm for counting connected components in the quadratic case than the general-purpose approach currently provides?
target_in_paper: Section 9, open problem "More Efficient Algorithms for Computing the Number of Connected Components in the Quadratic Case ?" (p. 69).
correct_elements: Your draft captures the right open problem almost exactly: the paper asks about counting the number of connected components, i.e. b_0(S), for semi-algebraic sets in R^k defined by ell quadratic inequalities, and whether the current k^(2^O(ell)) route coming from all-Betti-number algorithms can be improved to k^O(ell) or even k^O(ell^2) (Section 9, p. 69). It also correctly frames the question as asking for something substantially better than the known general-purpose all-Betti-number method summarized earlier in the survey (Section 3, p. 10).
missing_details: The paper is about the number of connected components b_0(S) of a basic closed semi-algebraic set given by a conjunction of quadratic inequalities; your draft says "semi-algebraic set defined by ell quadratic inequalities" but does not explicitly pin this down to a basic closed input of the form S = {x in R^k : P_1(x) >= 0, ..., P_ell(x) >= 0} or equivalently with <= 0 after sign changes (Section 9, p. 69; Theorem 7.22, p. 64).

The ambient space in the open problem is R^k. The survey’s general complexity model, however, is arithmetic complexity over the ordered ring generated by the input coefficients; your draft does not state that complexity is being measured in this sense (Definition 2.2, Section 2.2, p. 3).

The degree restriction should be stated explicitly as deg(P_i) <= 2 for each i. Your draft says "quadratic inequalities," which strongly suggests this, but the stand-alone version should make it explicit (Section 3, p. 10; Theorem 7.22, p. 64).

The paper compares this open problem not only against the all-Betti-number algorithm with k^(2^O(ell)) complexity, but also against the already-known k^O(ell) algorithms for emptiness, sample-point computation meeting every connected component, and Euler-Poincare characteristic. Those benchmarks are part of the intended context and are missing from the draft (Section 9, p. 69; Section 3, p. 10).

The paper adds an important negative methodological remark: roadmap-style methods used for general semi-algebraic sets do not directly solve this problem, because they would still be exponential in k in the quadratic setting. That caveat is omitted in the draft (Section 9, p. 69).

No homogeneity assumption is present here, and no boundedness assumption is imposed in the open problem as stated. The refined question should therefore not accidentally specialize to homogeneous, compact, or projected cases (Section 9, p. 69).

The paper does not formulate this as a question about arbitrary Boolean combinations, quantifier elimination, or projections; it is narrowly about counting connected components in the quadratic case itself. Your draft is close, but a fully stand-alone version should exclude those broader neighboring problems (Section 9, p. 69; compare Section 2.4.3, pp. 6-7).
refined_question: Let P_1, ..., P_ell in R[X_1, ..., X_k] be polynomials with deg(P_i) <= 2, and let S = {x in R^k : P_1(x) >= 0, ..., P_ell(x) >= 0} be the resulting basic closed semi-algebraic set. In the survey’s arithmetic-complexity model, is there an algorithm for computing b_0(S), the number of connected components of S, with complexity k^O(ell), or at least k^O(ell^2), rather than only via the currently available all-Betti-number approach yielding k^(2^O(ell))? Equivalently in the paper’s intended sense, can connected-component counting in the quadratic case be done substantially more efficiently than by invoking the known algorithm for all Betti numbers, given that general roadmap methods would still be exponential in k here?
justification: The draft clearly targets the Section 9 open problem rather than any introductory theorem: the distinctive fingerprints are the focus on connected components in the quadratic case, the explicit candidate bounds k^O(ell) and k^O(ell^2), and the comparison against the current k^(2^O(ell)) complexity coming from all-Betti-number methods (Section 9, p. 69). To make the question fully stand-alone and faithful to the survey, I made explicit the input class (a basic closed set in R^k given by ell quadratic inequalities), the exact invariant b_0(S), and the survey’s complexity model from Definition 2.2. I also kept the question narrow by not broadening it to projections, Boolean formulas, or higher-degree inputs, which are discussed elsewhere in the survey but are not the target of this open problem.
